content: The protective effect of treatment was more pronounced in individuals with a positive Tuberculin Skin Test (TST), showing a 49% reduction in tuberculosis (TB) disease and a 50% reduction in mortality. In those with a negative TST, the effects were not statistically significant, although there was an estimated 27% reduction in TB incidence. In two of the reviewed studies, antiretroviral therapy (ART) was not utilized, and in the third study, ART coverage was initially low but increased during the observation period. The recommendation for longer-term isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) is conditional and based on evidence that it provides significant additional benefits when combined with ART. The safety, efficacy, and convenience of repeated shorter rifapentine-based regimens are currently being studied in people living with HIV in similar settings. National authorities should define what constitutes a high TB transmission setting. Testing for TB infection is not a prerequisite for TB preventive treatment (TPT) in people living with HIV, but it is encouraged because individuals with a positive TST derive greater protective benefits from TPT. However, individuals with HIV and a negative TST should not receive 36 months of daily IPT. Special considerations should be made when selecting TPT regimens for people living with HIV. Rifamycins, for example, induce certain cytochrome P-450 enzymes, which can accelerate the elimination of medications metabolized through this pathway, including several antiretroviral drugs (ARVs). Rifampicin, in particular, can reduce the concentrations of antiretroviral agents such as atazanavir, darunavir, fosamprenavir, lopinavir, saquinavir, and tipranavir, and it should not be used with saquinavir/ritonavir. However, no dose adjustment is required when rifampicin is co-administered with efavirenz. The dose of dolutegravir (DTG) must be increased to 50 mg twice daily when given with rifampicin, a regimen that is generally well-tolerated and maintains equivalent efficacy in viral suppression and CD4 cell recovery compared to efavirenz. The 3HP regimen (once-weekly isoniazid and rifapentine for 12 weeks) can be safely administered to individuals on efavirenz-based antiretroviral regimens without dose adjustment, as shown in pharmacokinetic studies. Co-administration of rifapentine with raltegravir has also been found to be safe and well-tolerated. A drug interaction study involving DTG and once-weekly 3HP reported toxicities in two out of four participants, but more recent Phase 1/2 trial results in adults with HIV showed good tolerance, viral load suppression, and no significant adverse events related to 3HP. Additionally, rifapentine did not reduce DTG levels to a degree requiring dose adjustment. Pregnant women living with HIV are at increased risk for TB, which can have severe consequences for both the mother and fetus, including higher risks of maternal and infant mortality. Pregnancy should not disqualify women living with HIV from receiving preventive treatment with medications commonly used to treat TB, such as isoniazid and rifampicin, which are generally considered safe during pregnancy. However, data on the safety and efficacy of rifapentine during pregnancy remain limited. Based on these findings, the Guideline Development Group (GDG) concluded that there was insufficient evidence to change previous guidance or develop a separate recommendation for IPT use in pregnant women living with HIV. Systematic deferral of IPT to the postpartum period would deprive women of its protective benefits during a time of heightened vulnerability to TB. Concurrent use of alcohol should be avoided during TPT. Further details on drug-drug interactions for TPT and TB treatment regimens are available in the WHO operational handbook on tuberculosis. Administrative controls include triaging individuals with TB symptoms or disease to reduce transmission to healthcare workers and others in high-risk settings. Respiratory separation or isolation of individuals with presumed or confirmed infectious TB is recommended to further reduce transmission. Prompt initiation of effective TB treatment is also strongly recommended to minimize transmission risks. Respiratory hygiene, including cough etiquette, is advised for individuals with presumed or confirmed TB. Environmental controls aim to prevent the spread of infectious respiratory particles and reduce their concentration. Recommended interventions include the use of upper-room germicidal ultraviolet (GUV) systems and maximizing ventilation through natural, mixed-mode, or mechanical systems, as well as recirculating air through high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filters. Routine HIV testing services should be offered to all individuals with presumptive or diagnosed TB, as well as to household contacts of people with HIV-associated TB. In high HIV-burden settings, all household and close contacts of individuals with TB should be offered HIV testing services. In low HIV-burden settings, HIV testing may be offered to household members and close contacts of TB patients who exhibit symptoms compatible with TB disease. Partner services should also be offered to individuals with HIV-associated TB to extend HIV testing, prevention, and treatment services to their sexual partners and household members. For people living with HIV diagnosed with TB, a package of interventions, including screening, treatment, and/or prophylaxis for major opportunistic infections, rapid ART initiation, and intensified adherence support, should be provided. ART should be initiated as soon as possible within two weeks of starting TB treatment, regardless of CD4 cell count, except in cases of TB meningitis, where ART initiation should be delayed by at least four weeks due to safety concerns. Routine co-trimoxazole prophylaxis should also be given to all people living with HIV with active TB disease, regardless of CD4 cell count. Advanced HIV disease, defined as a CD4 cell count of less than 200 cells/mm³ or WHO clinical stage 3 or 4 disease, is associated with a high risk of mortality, even after starting ART. To address the leading causes of morbidity and mortality in this population, WHO recommends an integrated package of care, including screening, treatment, and prophylaxis for major opportunistic infections, rapid ART initiation, and adherence support interventions. TB and HIV programs are encouraged to collaborate to expand access to this integrated care package for people with advanced HIV disease and TB.
